race_context: The Crown Point Community School Corporation is a PreK–12 district serving about 9,000 students from Crown Point and parts of Winfield and Cedar Lake {cpcsc_ilearn}. Residents of Center and Winfield townships may speak at board meetings {cpcsc_board}. It runs seven elementary schools, two middle schools (Col. Wheeler and Taft) and Crown Point High School {cpcsc_board}{wiki_cpcsc}. Dr. Todd Terrill has been superintendent since July 2020 {cpcsc_admin}{wiki_cpcsc}.

The board has five members: two elected at large and one each from Districts 1, 2 and 3 {lc_directory}. Every voter in the district votes in all of the board races on the ballot, as the county's sample ballots for both Crown Point and Winfield Township precincts show {lc_sample_cp}{lc_sample_wt}. The current members are President Brian Smith, Vice President Danielle Bazin, Scott Angel, Secretary David Warne and Tom Hoffman {cpcsc_board}.

Seats on the 2026 ballot: one at-large seat and the District 1 seat, each 'Vote For One (1) Only,' which matches the state list {lc_sample_cp}. Both seats were last filled in 2022, when Timothy Vassar won at large and Danielle Bazin won District 1 {lc_results_2022}{lc_directory}.

At-large seat: after Vassar resigned, the board appointed former member Thomas Hoffman on June 22, 2026 to serve through Dec. 31, 2026 {cpcsc_recap_jun26}. Hoffman is not on the 2026 candidate list {lc_candidates}. The candidates are Bazin, who now holds District 1, and Bill Muha {lc_sample_cp}.

District 1 seat: Bazin is running at large instead of for reelection in District 1, so Anne Annie Equihua is the only District 1 candidate {lc_candidates}{lc_sample_cp}. Whichever race Bazin wins or loses, the board will have at least one new member in January 2027.
Not on this ballot: Smith (at large), Warne (District 2) and Angel (District 3) won their seats in 2024, and their terms run through 2028 {lc_results_2024}{lc_directory}.

Operating referendum on the same ballot (2026): on June 22, 2026 the board voted to put an operating referendum on the November ballot to make up revenue lost under Senate Enrolled Act 1 {cpcsc_recap_jun26}. The ballot question asks for up to 38.7 cents per $100 of assessed value and up to $19,750,000 a year for eight years, and states that the annual bill on a $350,000 median home would rise $648 {lc_sample_cp}. The district says the new rate would replace the 18-cent referendum voters approved in 2025, not add to it. It projects that the actual bill on a $317,000 median home would rise $7 in 2027 and fall $265 in 2028 as SEA 1 deductions grow {cpcsc_recap_sep26}.

Budget and SEA 1 (2025–2026): the district says SEA 1 cost it about $2 million in 2025 and nearly $4 million in 2026, and projects nearly $5 million by 2029 {cpcsc_recap_sep26}. It says it made $7.3 million in cuts last year, including about $2.1 million from the state taking over curricular-materials funding and more than $5 million from a special education operating loss, as special education enrollment grew more than 34% in five years {cpcsc_recap_sep26}. If the referendum fails, the district projects cutting an estimated 50–60 certified positions plus 10–15 referendum-funded positions in the first year, along with cuts to transportation {cpcsc_recap_sep26}. The advertised 2027 maximum budget is $140,789,316 {cpcsc_recap_sep26}.

Fund transfers (2025–2026): the board approved moving $1 million from the Rainy Day Fund in December 2025 and $2.5 million in May 2026, which left a projected Rainy Day balance of about $5.3 million {cpcsc_recap_dec25}{cpcsc_recap_may26}. In July 2026 it made a one-time transfer of $1.8 million from debt service to operations, allowed by a 2025 state law (HEA 1210) {cpcsc_recap_jul26}.
Facilities (2026): in July 2026 the board approved issuing $5 million in general obligation bonds for HVAC work, transportation and buses {cpcsc_recap_jul26}.

Academics (2026): the district reports that among Indiana's 30 traditional public districts with at least 4,000 students in grades 3–8, it ranked fourth in math and sixth in English/language arts on 2026 ILEARN results {cpcsc_ilearn}.

Other 2025–2026 board items: in December 2025 parents raised concerns about class sizes and a land swap at 129th Avenue and Iowa Street, and board members responded that the land decisions followed required legal processes {cpcsc_recap_dec25}. In May 2026 the board adopted a policy, required by a new state law, that personal devices be powered off and stored during the school day {cpcsc_recap_may26}. In June 2026 it approved a three-year strategic plan framework {cpcsc_recap_jun26}.
Forums: this guide found no candidate forums, questionnaires or news coverage of the 2026 Crown Point race. The Times of Northwest Indiana (nwitimes.com) could not be read for this guide.
